items.title: Tems sets new record for longest-charting solo African song on Billboard Hot 100
items.description: Nigerian singer Temilade Openiyi, popularly known as Tems, has set a new record for the longest-charting solo song by an African act on the US Billboard Hot 100. Her hit song ‘What You Need’ charts another week on the Billboard Hot 100, bringing its total to 30 weeks. Consequently, it has now surpassed South African pop star Tyla’s ‘Water’ and Afrobeats singer CKay’s ‘Love Nwantiti’ (29 weeks) as the longest-charting solo African song on the Billboard Hot 100 Chart. ‘What You Need’ is charting at number 33 this week. The song peaked at number 29 on the Billboard Hot 100 Chart. It reached number 1 on Billboard’s Mainstream R&B/Hip-Hop Airplay and Adult R&B Airplay charts.

items.title: Commerce numérique : Zoom sur « le Chinois du Burkina », le commerçant qui attire 1,1 million de fans sur TikTok
items.description: Il s'appelle Macaire Yaméogo, il vend des smartphones dans le quartier Koulouba de Ouagadougou, et son apprenrce lui a valu un surnom qui lui confère deux nationalités : le Chinois du Burkina. Grâce à ses talents d'animateur, il fédère plus d'un million cent mille abonnés sur TikTok autour de l'humour et de la promotion de ses produits. La façade de la boutique de l'intéressée le distingue déjà. En plus de l'ecritau «Chinois du Burkina », qu'on peut apercevoir aisément, deux drapeaux flottent au dessus de la boutique : celui du Burkina Faso et celui de la Chine. Une fois introduit dans la boutique, nous voyons l'homme pour la première fois et… il ressemble vraiment à un Chinois ! Les pommettes hautes, le regard légèrement bridé et le teint clair qui intrigue et qui amusent à la fois. Habitué depuis longtemps à être le premier sujet d'étonnement de quiconque le croise pour la première fois, il nous accueille aussi avec le sourire réciproquement amusé. La boutique bourdonne. Assis sur le comptoir, le jeune commerçant jongle entre plusieurs conversations à la fois : un employé qui lui rappelle un achat à effectuer, un autre qui lui rapporte des faits divers tirés des réseaux sociaux, un client qui hésite entre deux modèles. Peu après, Macaire se lève pour superviser le déballage de plusieurs cartons de smartphones qui lui ont été livrés. Chaque appareil dans son carton est ensuite exposé sur les étagères de la boutique, déjà garnis de diverses gammes de téléphones. C'est seulement une fois le stock rangé et catalogué qu'il nous fait signe de le rejoindre dans son bureau. Tout a commencé en 2014, quand Macaire débute la vente des téléphones pour le compte d'autrui, sans boutique propre. Il faut attendre 2024 pour qu'il franchisse le pas et ouvre son propre espace à Koulouba. Entre-temps, sa ressemblance physique avec les ressortissants chinois lui vaut un sobriquet qui devient une marque. « Si on part en Chine, même les Chinois se confondent. Ils pensent que je suis leur collègue. Donc je me suis nommé Chinois du Burkina. Ça veut dire un Burkinabè qui représente la Chine » , raconte-t-il en riant. TikTok, le comptoir qui ne ferme jamais La vraie révolution pour Macaire Yaméogo, c'est TikTok. Vendeur le jour, animateur la nuit, il lance des lives à 21h qui durent jusqu'à minuit, où il mélange présentation de produits, humour et bonne humeur contagieuse. Par exemple, il organise un concours en mooré. La règle du jeu est simple : parler cinq minutes en mooré sans glisser un seul mot français, même pas « ça va » ni « OK ». Les meilleurs gagnent des cadeaux. Trois à quatre par jour, selon lui. « Notre Président a dit de valoriser notre langue. Moi, je suis mooré à 100 %. Tout le monde doit parler mooré » , explique-t-il. Résultat, le compte TikTok du Chinois du Burkina affiche plus d'un million cent mille abonnés et 21,3 millions de mentions « J'aime ». Des chiffres qui ne garantissent pas mécaniquement des ventes, mais qui offrent à sa boutique physique une vitrine. L'honnêteté comme argument commercial Dans un secteur où la frontière entre le faux et le vrai est souvent floue, Macaire Yaméogo joue la carte de la transparence. « Quand le téléphone n'est pas original, on dit au client que ce n'est pas original. Quand c'est original, on le dit aussi. On ne peut pas prendre une copie et faire croire que c'est de l'original » , tranche-t-il. Une garantie de retour est systématiquement proposée au cas où un problème survient. Cette politique de confiance, doublée d'une présence quotidienne sur les réseaux, a construit une clientèle qui n'hésite pas à passer commande depuis des localités éloignées. Les défis d'un métier qui ne pardonne pas les stocks dormants Derrière l'humour et les lives, Macaire Yaméogo ne cache pas la réalité de son commerce. Le marché des smartphones obéit à la logique de la fluctuation des prix. Un appareil acheté à Dubaï à 100 000 FCFA peut se retrouver à 90 000 FCFA sur le marché mondial un mois plus tard, laissant le revendeur avec un stock dévalué sur les bras. « Chaque domaine a sa difficulté, mais il faut être honnête. Si tu commences avec la vérité, tu verras qu'avec le temps, tu auras plus de clients que ceux qui ont commencé dans le mensonge » , philosophe-t-il. Dans un Burkina Faso où le commerce informel se réinvente sur les plateformes numériques, le cas de Macaire Yaméogo montre que la boutique physique et la communauté en ligne ne sont plus deux mondes séparés pour faire du business. Le Chinois du Burkina en a fait un modèle, avec ses propres codes. Josué TIENDREBEOGO Faso7 L’article Commerce numérique : Zoom sur « le Chinois du Burkina », le commerçant qui attire 1,1 million de fans sur TikTok est apparu en premier sur Faso7 .

items.title: Opération « zéro poulailler vide » : des poules et des aliments pour volaille remis aux fermiers à Mogdin et à Gampéla
items.description: Le ministre délégué chargé des Ressources animales, Amadou Dicko, a remis des kits composés de poules et d’aliments pour volaille à des fermiers de Mogdin et de Gampéla dans la commune de Saaba, jeudi 22 octobre 2026. L’opération « zéro poulailler vide » est en marche. En effet, le ministre délégué chargé des Ressources animales, Amadou Dicko, a visité deux fermes avicoles à Mogdin et à Gampéla dans la commune de Saaba, à la périphérie Est de Ouaga-dougou, jeudi 22 octobre 2026. Il a, à l’occasion, remis des kits composés de poules et d’aliments pour volaille aux fermiers de ces localités. A Mogdin, le fermier Abdoul Razack Seni a remercié le ministère de l’Agriculture, de l’Eau, des Ressources animales et halieutiques pour l’initiative. « Le Burkina Faso a vraiment besoin de cette opération. Ces poulets locaux améliorés vont nous permettre d’accroitre la production avicole dans notre Centre de formation professionnelle agricole Baôba (CFP-AGB) », a-t-il déclaré. Il a ajouté que c’est l’occasion pour son centre de montrer à ses apprenants comment réceptionner les poulets et les entretenir jusqu’à maturité. Satisfécit des aviculteurs Abdoul Razack Seni a, par ailleurs, rappelé que le CFP-AGB a été créé en juillet 2025 et a formé au total 100 personnes (formation initiale et de courte durée), en collaboration avec la délégation spéciale de Saaba. La fermière de Gampéla, Mamounata Kaboré, a également témoi-gné sa satisfaction d’être sélectionnée dans la dyna-mique de l’opération « zéro poulailler vide ». « Je suis une nouvelle retraitée et je produis depuis 2024. Mais, par la suite, j’ai enregistré des difficultés. Je salue cette action concrète de l’Etat burkinabè », a-t-elle signifié. Elle a confié que pour le moment, elle est bénéficiaire de 35 sacs d’aliments de volaille, en attendant les poulets. Quant au directeur général des productions animales, Emilien Bakoné, il a soutenu que l’opération « zéro poulailler vide », lancée le 21 août 2026, s’inscrit dans le cadre de l’Offensive agropastorale, hydraulique et halieutique 2026-2028. « C’est une première initiative de pouvoir renforcer les capacités d’au moins 500 aviculteurs modernes et traditionnels en leur dotant de kits », a-t-il laissé entendre. Sur le plan de l’élevage moderne, aux dires de Emilien Bakoné, il est prévu d’offrir à chaque bénéficiaire un kit de 1 000 poussins de chair et de plus de deux tonnes d’aliments de volaille ainsi qu’un appui en vaccin. « Pour ce qui est de l’élevage traditionnel, le kit était de 100 volailles adultes composés de 90 poules et 10 coqs avec un accompagnement d’aliments de volaille de trois tonnes et de soins vétérinaires », a-t-il fait comprendre. Le directeur général des productions animales a aussi fait savoir que 24 000 personnes se sont inscrites sur la plateforme du ministère en charge de l’agriculture après le lancement de l’opération « zéro poulailler vide ». « A l’issue de la sélection, 516 bénéficiaires ont été retenus et présentés au public », a relevé Emilien Bakoné. Pingdebwoaga Urielle Lauryn KABORE

items.title: US actor Tom Skerritt, who starred in Top Gun, Steel Magnolias and Alien, dies aged 93
items.description: US actor Tom Skerritt, who starred in the TV series Picket Fences and the films Alien and Top Gun, has died aged 93, his family says. Skerritt died on Wednesday of natural causes, his family said: “While the world knew Tom through his remarkable acting career, we knew him for his humour, curiosity, wisdom, generosity, and the love he brought into our lives.” Over a six-decade career, he took on film and TV roles, including Mash, A River Runs Through It, and Ted. He also co-founded TheFilmSchool in Seattle to support next-generation filmmakers and storytellers. His family said he will be remembered “for his belief that stories can help people heal, find purpose, and create change”. Actor Tom Skerritt in a scene from the movie ‘Alien’ in 1979 The moustachioed star of several 20th century hit films was born in 1933 in Detroit, Michigan, and served in the US Air Force before pursuing an acting career that boasted several military roles. He made his film debut in 1962 alongside a young Robert Redford in War Hunt and, years later, re-teamed with Redford in the 1992 period drama A River Runs Through It, which starred Brad Pitt. Skerritt’s breakthrough role came when he played US army surgeon Duke Forrest in the 1970 Korean War comedy Mash, which also starred Donald Sutherland, Elliott Gould and Sally Kellerman. Released amid unrest over the Vietnam War, the hit film earned five Academy Award nominations and was adapted for television two years later. He also starred alongside Sigourney Weaver in the 1979 sci-fi film Alien, which earned two Oscar nominations, and led to three sequels and several crossover projects. “It is spontaneity and impulse ​that make the difference, and that is ⁠what I felt we had with ‘Alien,'” Skerritt said in a 2019 interview, according to Reuters news agency. “Every one of us had that immediate rapport with each other.” Skerritt said that one of the things he liked most when he first read the script was that “the woman becomes a hero”, referring to Weaver’s character, Ripley. During his career, he starred opposite several strong female leads. He appeared with Shirley MacLaine in the 1977 film Turning Point and played Sally Field’s husband in 1989’s Steel Magnolias. Skerritt starred with Julia Roberts in the film Steel Magnolias As Commander Mike “Viper” Metcalf in the 1986 classic Top Gun, the versatile actor appeared alongside a young Tom Cruise in the blockbuster. On television, he won an Emmy Award in 1993 for his role as Sheriff Jimmy Brock in David E Kelley’s drama Picket Fences. The quirky procedural’s ensemble cast was nominated for SAG Awards in 1995 and 1996, and he received a nod for male actor in a drama series in 1995. Picket Fences star Lauren Holly, who played Skerritt’s deputy on Picket Fences, described him in a tribute as “our leader”. “His example made those years such a joy and we all loved and respected him so much,” Holly wrote, adding: “He cared deeply for his family-both the one at home and the one at work. He cared deeply for his planet, and all of its inhabitants. He had a huge impact on my life, and so many memories I have of him include sharing fits of crippling laughter.” Skerritt also had guest roles on the small screen in The West Wing, Madam Secretary, Law & Order: SVU and Huff. He reteamed with Field as the family patriarch, William Walker, in the drama Brothers & Sisters from 2007-09. He had a six-episode stint on Cheers playing Rebecca Howe’s crush-worthy boss Evan Drake. In a statement, Skerritt’s family said that he leaves behind a “legacy that reaches far beyond the screen”. A deep believer in the power of storytelling, Skerritt helped found the TheFilmSchool in Seattle and co-founded the Red Badge Project, which helps veterans work through PTSD, anxiety and depression by writing and sharing their experiences. Inspired in part by his experience filming A River Runs Through It, he also believed in protecting the natural world. He created the documentary series Reflections of the River about America’s rivers and supported river conservation. Skerrit is survived by his third wife Julie, five children and several grandchildren. Skerritt was seen with fellow actors Joan Collins, Morgan Freeman and Jessica Tandy and at the 47th Golden Globe Awards in January 1990

items.title: Meta veut lever des centaines de milliards de dollars pour accélérer dans l’IA
items.description: Porté par la croissance de ses revenus publicitaires, Meta prépare une vaste opération de financement pour renforcer ses ambitions dans l’intelligence artificielle. Le groupe de Mark Zuckerberg prévoit de créer de nouvelles actions sans droit de vote afin d’attirer des investisseurs tout en préservant le contrôle de son fondateur. Meta prépare une opération financière de grande ampleur pour accélérer dans l’intelligence artificielle (IA). Le groupe américain entend lever des centaines de milliards de dollars sur plusieurs années afin de rivaliser avec OpenAI, Google et Anthropic, sans remettre en cause le pouvoir décisionnel de son fondateur, Mark Zuckerberg. Dévoilé mercredi 21 octobre, le mécanisme envisagé repose sur la création de nouvelles actions dépourvues de droits de vote. Cette structure permettrait à Meta de mobiliser des capitaux supplémentaires sans diluer le contrôle exercé par son dirigeant sur l’entreprise. Cette stratégie intervient alors que le groupe poursuit des investissements massifs dans l’IA, un secteur devenu central dans la compétition entre les grandes entreprises technologiques. Meta dispose d’une activité publicitaire particulièrement dynamique. Au troisième trimestre 2026, son chiffre d’affaires a atteint 64,6 milliards de dollars, en progression de 26 % sur un an, porté notamment par les revenus générés sur Facebook, Instagram et WhatsApp. Le résultat dépasse les attentes du marché. Le bénéfice du groupe a toutefois été affecté par une charge de près de 10 milliards de dollars liée à un accord conclu fin août avec la quasi-totalité des États américains, dans le cadre de poursuites portant sur les effets potentiellement addictifs de ses plateformes auprès des adolescents. Meta reste également confronté à plusieurs procédures judiciaires aux États-Unis. Des familles et des districts scolaires poursuivent le groupe, tandis qu’un juge du Nouveau-Mexique lui a infligé une amende de 25 milliards de dollars dans une affaire liée à la protection des données personnelles et à Cambridge Analytica. Malgré ces risques, les perspectives financières restent solides. L’entreprise prévoit un chiffre d’affaires compris entre 73 et 76 milliards de dollars au quatrième trimestre. The post Meta veut lever des centaines de milliards de dollars pour accélérer dans l’IA appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Powerful earthquake hits Tibet killing 16 people, reports say
items.description: A magnitude seven earthquake has hit a mountainous region in Tibet, killing at least 16 people and injuring dozens of others, according to Chinese state media reports. The centre of the quake hit Baqên County in the Nagqu regionas on Thursday night, Xinhua reported, citing the local emergency management bureau. The county – located in what China calls the Tibet Autonomous Region after annexing it in the 1950s – is 400km north-east of the region’s capital, Lhasa. Authorities have declared an emergency and deployed rescue teams to the affected area, where 32 others have also been injured. Power has been cut off and 339 homes have collapsed in the affected region, local reports said. Rockfall has forced roads in the region to close, making it more difficult for crews to reach impacted high-altitude areas. Strong tremors were also felt in the cities of Qamdo and Nyingchi in Tibet. Videos on social media show villagers running into the streets as buildings shake violently in the dark, although these have not been independently verified. The region is prone to devastating seismic activity. In 2023, a 6.2 magnitude quake killed more than 120 people in the nearby mountainous Gansu province of China. Tibet and Nepal were also recently devastated by massive floods and landslides less than two months ago, unleashed by a glacier collapse, which killed at least 1,400 people. Hundreds of others are still reported missing. Tibet, which has long demanded greater autonomy, is one of the most tightly controlled regions in China. With foreign media restricted from the region and information heavily censored by authorities, Chinese state media is the main source for updates and details when such disasters happen.

items.title: SIAO 2026 : la LONAB injecte 50 millions F CFA pour l’organisation
items.description: La Loterie nationale burkinabè (LONAB) apporte son soutien à l’organisation du 18e Salon international de l’artisanat de Ouagadougou (SIAO) à hauteur de 50 millions F CFA. Cet appui financier a fait l’objet d’une signature de convention entre les deux institutions, le jeudi 22 octobre 2026, à Ouagadougou. Traditionnel partenaire du Salon international de l’artisanat de Ouagadougou (SIAO), la Loterie nationale burkinabé (LONAB) a, une fois de plus, marqué sa disponibilité à accompa-gner ce rendez-vous international de l’artisanat africain. Pour l’organisation de cette 18e édition SIAO, qui se tient du 30 octobre au 8 novembre 2026, dans la capitale burkinabè, sur le thème, « Artisanat africain et industrialisation : quelle synergie pour une meilleure valorisation des produits locaux et du patrimoine culturel », en tant que sponsor officiel, la Nationale des jeux a décidé d’apporter un soutien financier à hauteur de 50 millions F CFA. Cet appui a fait l’objet d’une signature de convention entre les deux structures, le jeudi 22 octobre, à Ouagadougou. Selon le directeur général de la LONAB, Ibrahim Ben Harouna Zarani, cette contribution financière de 50 millions F CFA traduit la volonté de sa structure à accompagner la réussite de cet évènement majeur. Il a relevé que le SIAO contribue à révéler le talent, le savoir-faire et à créer des emplois, à générer des revenus et à valoriser l’identité culturelle du Burkina Faso voire de l’Afrique. « Cet engagement de la LONAB est en parfaite cohérence avec notre plan stratégique révisé 2023-2027, notamment son axe relatif au développement socio-écono-mique et à la promotion des initiatives créatrices de valeurs au profit des populations », a-t-il souligné. Cette collaboration, a-t-il poursuivi, s’appuie sur une histoire de confiance réciproque entre les deux partenaires et sur la réussite des éditions passées. Il est convaincu que lorsque les institutions nationales travaillent ensemble, les résultats suivent. En contrepartie de cet appui, la LONAB bénéficiera d’un espace de promotion et de vente de ses produits. Ibrahim Ben Harouna Zarani a salué le travail qu’abat au quotidien le comité d’organisation du SIAO, tout en formulant le vœu que cette édition connaisse un succès et contribue davantage à la promotion du savoir-faire burkinabè et au rayonnement de l’artisanat africain. Le directeur général du Salon international de l’artisanat de Ouagadougou, Eric Bassolé, a confié que cet apport financier va contribuer à faire face à beaucoup de défis rencontrés sur le site du SIAO. Il traduit sa gratitude à la LONAB qui accompagne le SIAO depuis plu-sieurs éditions, tout en lançant un appel aux sociétés d’Etat ainsi que celles du privé à emboiter le pas de ce partenaire afin de faire briller davantage l’artisanat africain, et en particulier burkinabè. Mahamadi SEBOGO Aïssatou DIARRA (Stagiaire)

items.title: ‘If Anything Happens to This Guy … Everyone Is Screwed’
items.description: On Tuesday, the world found out about two massive security vulnerabilities in PHP, a programming language that is used by roughly 70 percent of websites. The flaw was discovered by cybersecurity researchers using a frontier model from OpenAI. If they exploited it, attackers could gain full control of servers, stealing or copying anything inside or simply taking sites offline. The PHP Foundation, the organization that maintains the programming language, had recently learned about the security flaws, but the disclosure was leaked on a forum before a patch could be released. What happened next was a frantic race with numerous participants: the foundation, which needed to create and release a patch; developers around the world, who would need to deploy it; and attackers looking to exploit these vulnerabilities in the interim. Matthew Prince, the CEO of the hosting company Cloudflare, wrote that in the 10 hours before the flaws were publicly announced, “we saw thousands of attempts to exploit it. That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within 2 hours, and millions now.” Once the patch was released yesterday, websites everywhere went offline to implement the fix. These included government websites in Germany and Finland, some hospital and school websites in Europe, and international sites such as 4chan. During this race to secure the majority of the internet, I noticed one name pop up in posts on Reddit and X: Ondřej Surý. “Explaining to my wife how there’s this one guy. And he alone is responsible for most of the world’s distribution of PHP,” a software developer named Ian Landsman wrote on X. “And if anything happens to this guy, that’s just it. Everyone is screwed.” He was referring to Surý. Surý, who lives in Czechia, does not work for the PHP Foundation. But alongside his day job as director of domain-name-system engineering at the nonprofit Internet Systems Consortium, in a volunteer capacity, he maintains and helps automate patches for the coding language. His work, with that of just a handful of others, has allowed countless websites and organizations to fix these vulnerabilities quickly. Over the past 48 hours, he’s become arguably the unsung hero of the entire internet—despite the fact that the only compensation he receives is from modest donations. “Ondřej will save the internet today,” a user in the PHP Subreddit wrote. I spoke with Surý today from his home about the unfolding AI-cybersecurity crisis, how the internet’s infrastructure is maintained by small crews of volunteers such as himself, and how it feels to go to bed after saving the web as we know it. Our conversation has been edited for length and clarity. Charlie Warzel: Explain to me what has happened in layman’s terms over the past 72 hours. Ondřej Surý: Earlier this week, I got notified by the PHP project that there was a serious security vulnerability in the coding. On Tuesday, it became apparent that someone had leaked information about the upcoming vulnerabilities, and it was decided inside the PHP project that it needed to accelerate the release process from Thursday to Wednesday. This is when it became a little bit crazy, because now we were one day short suddenly. Warzel: I want to try to put this into perspective: So basically, the PHP programming language that kind of undergirds the web is used by up to 70 percent of websites? Surý: That’s what I heard as well. Warzel: So people search for cybersecurity vulnerabilities, not necessarily for offensive-attack opportunities but maybe just defensive opportunities. And someone found a vulnerability—that’s not super abnormal. But the real issue here was how widely it was disclosed and the amount of time before people had to patch this, right? Surý: Let me clarify that: It’s the severity. The severity is unusual. Remote Code Execution is the most severe type of vulnerability, because the attacker is able to execute their own code on the server that’s running PHP. That’s why this caused such panic throughout the internet. As you said, if about 70 percent of websites are running PHP, the impact would be huge if attackers would actually be able to execute code on these servers. Warzel: You said that despite the panic online, it has not been a crazy 48 hours. From the outside, that’s surprising. I keep seeing people saying, There’s one person who is in charge of fixing this—and he’s supporting himself through Patreon . They may have been exaggerating, but there’s some truth to that: Your work was single-handedly helping millions of people. How could this not be a crazy time for you? Surý: There are a couple of reasons. One is that I’ve been doing this for a long time, over 20 years. A lot of the stuff that I do is automated. But the reason it was not crazy for me was that I actually don’t have any system running PHP myself. So for me, it was like, sure, I feel a responsibility toward the users of the internet. It would be a crazy day for me if I was on a boat in the middle of the Adriatic Sea. That could happen. But I had time to prepare the packages. Warzel: That’s kinda wild. Surý: And even without me, people would still be able to get PHP from other sources and compile it themselves. But it would be more complicated for everyone. And some people don’t immediately have the skill to upgrade the PHP. What the PHP project did was release the source code for the language. What I am doing is preparing it into these things called packages that people can install on their servers. It’s very convenient, and it’s faster, and you can automate it and can install the same package over hundreds and thousands of servers, and you don’t have to compile it. If I was not available, it would take more time; some of them wouldn’t have the skills. Really, the thanks go to the PHP project that invited me into this secret cabal who knew about the vulnerabilities and had access before the public release. Warzel: When you got invited, was it a real Oh, crap moment for you? Surý: I’m in the stage of my life where I was like, This is bad . It needs to be fixed . But it doesn’t cause panic, at least for me. It did cause panic for a lot of people. But you know, it was more like, We have a situation, it needs to be solved, and this is how we do it. And I have time to properly prepare . If I didn’t have time to properly prepare, then it would cause a lot of stress. From where I stand, it was not stressful, because I’m doing this as a volunteer, and if I get hit by a bus, then it will be someone else’s problem. Warzel: Every time I dabble in writing about the world of cybersecurity and open-source software, I discover these groups of maintainers: people such as yourself who do this work because they care. Often, nobody knows their name. But is there a line of people who would take your place if, say, you did get hit by a bus? Surý: I am actually thinking about contingency plans. And we are talking with Raphaël Hertzog from the software company Freexian . My advantage is that I have a lot of expertise, and I know where to touch the thing to make it work. But Freexian has a lot of expertise, and they would be able to take over if anything happens. People have been donating small amounts, and larger amounts, like crazy since yesterday. I would like to thank them all. Warzel: Have the donations been overwhelming? Surý: Not Silicon Valley levels of money, but I got a serious amount of contributions that I’ve never seen before. It’s like one year of the contributions gathered over the past 24 hours. [ Matteo Wong: Read this website while you still can ] Warzel: What would have happened if this wasn’t patched as quickly as it was? Surý: A lot of things could have happened. The very basic thing is that there would be vandalism, that the sites would be taken down. And we are seeing this every day on the internet now. The other stuff that happens is that someone gets access and runs a botnet out of these devices. I would say it’s mostly organized crime doing that now—it’s not like a small guy in the basement doing this for fun. There are financial incentives for these people to sell the botnet services or to do the crypto-mining on these servers for a profit. And this still could happen, because it’s not like everyone has patched and updated their PHP. Warzel: I saw a post on X that said not all PHP releases are patched, and one-third of the internet is kind of permanently either broken or vulnerable. Is that correct? Surý: That initial information is not correct. There are ways to patch even the old versions. Warzel: So one-third of the internet is not permanently screwed. Okay. Surý: No, that’s not accurate. If people care enough, they are able to even update these old versions of PHP. Warzel: It’s a scary moment for cybersecurity. I’ve seen people online referring to this vulnerability and other AI-agent hacks as “ Black October ,” and there’s concern that defensive or attacking agents can find these vulnerabilities. There is this feeling that I am noticing from the cybersecurity community that their fears of a future where things are being exploited or discovered quicker than people can handle is coming true—that we are living in that moment. And then separately, there’s a contingent of people who are saying there is an equilibrium here: If you have very persistent agents that are very good at identifying and exploiting vulnerabilities, you also have very persistent agents that are very good at defending against them. Surý: What we’ve seen is that things have accelerated—that’s absolutely right. The defenders are also able to use the large language models to find the vulnerabilities for themselves. I believe it boils down to the simple fact that IT infrastructure is often being taken for granted. There’s not enough priority and money going to properly maintain the IT infrastructure in various places. It’s not only companies; it’s also a lot of outdated consumer electronics that are going to be attacked. I kind of agree that everything’s moving fast now, and it’s taking a toll on the people who are defending the stuff. At the same time, maybe this is the turning point where we actually start caring about this. [ Ian Bogost: Invasion of the self-replicating AI-malware botnet ] Warzel: Do you feel like that will actually happen? Surý: I might be wrong, but I’m an optimist that people will finally realize that we can’t go like this forever. This has been a disaster waiting to happen for a really, really long time. And this is just one of the many wake-up calls that came and will be coming. Warzel: I am amazed by how much the infrastructure in certain areas of the internet can hinge on one or two people. There is a fragility to all of this that is concerning. So what do you want to see? Surý: When I started doing open-source, it was fun. And it kind of still is. But the environment has shifted. Open-source sometimes feels like exploitation. What I would like to see is to find a new model where people working on open-source would be awarded for their work and the hours and hours they put into it from the people who most benefit from their work. I would like companies to realize that this is exploitation. Any exploitation is not sustainable. And it will end up badly if this continues, because the people doing the open-source will stop being motivated to actually do anything in the end. Warzel: It sounds like you don’t have an ego about all of this. But you did some work, and you helped out a tremendous amount of people in every corner of the world yesterday. How did it feel to go to bed last night after all of that, knowing the role that you played? Surý: Well, my wife says that I’m emotionally dead, but I’m not. And it felt nice. Like, seeing my social network filling up with thank-you notes, and getting emails with thank-yous, that feels really nice. It puts some sense into what I do. I felt that what I do has a purpose. Warzel: The whole internet appreciates your efforts. Is there anything that you would recommend normal people do at this moment to improve their internet hygiene? Surý: I would recommend that they rely on the experts. That’s what we all do in a crisis: We talk to experts and trust them. Rely on people, that people who take care of this stuff know what they are doing. And that’s all we can do.

items.title: Le rendez-vous manqué
items.description: Ce matin, j’ai attendu l’Afrique sur le quai de l’avenir Elle vrombissait au loin dans un nuage de poussière Les yeux larmoyant de joie, j’ai cru en elle avec zèle Elle vociférait dans la nuée ardente des volcans gênants Ce matin, je l’ai vue marcher, tanguant à pas de charge Ployant sous son propre poids et portant des faix défaits En tombant de partout, ses membres s’érodaient en l’air L’heure était grave sur le chemin de toutes les entraves Ce matin, j’ai vu l’Afrique debout sur des crics en briques Sa posture inclinée vers l’Ouest la brisait en deux au centre Pendant qu’au Sud, elle se donnait des coups de sa corne Sur son flanc Nord, les boussoles avaient perdu les repères Ce matin, elle est arrivée dans un berceau de mort-né Dépouillée par la portée agitée de l’espoir reporté Elle ne repartira peut-être demain peut-être pas ou jamais A deux mains, demain, remettons l’Afrique en chemin ! Clément ZONGO clmentzongo@yahoo.fr

items.title: Psychiatrists seek home-grown research to tackle Africa’s mental health crisis
items.description: … Say Nigeria’s Mental Health Act needs action, not just legislation By Chioma Obinna Nigeria and other African countries must invest in home-grown mental health research and translate policies into action to improve care for millions of people facing mental health challenges, psychiatrists have said. The experts warned that Africa’s low contribution to global mental health research was limiting the continent’s capacity to develop evidence-based responses suited to its population, while weak implementation of policies threatened to widen the gap between legislation and access to care. They spoke at the ninth International Research Conference of the Federal Neuro-Psychiatric Hospital, Yaba, Lagos, themed, “Mental Health Research at the Crossroads: Challenges, Policies and Reforms in Africa.” Professor Taiwo Lateef Sheikh, a professor of psychiatry at Ahmadu Bello University, Zaria, said Africa accounted for less than two per cent of global mental health research output, a situation he said underscored the urgent need to strengthen local research capacity. Sheikh called for increased investment in African-led studies, arguing that research priorities should reflect the realities of local communities and provide evidence for policies and interventions. He also drew attention to the implementation gap surrounding Nigeria’s Mental Health Act, stressing that the existence of a law was not enough without concrete action, institutional commitment and adequate resources. For Nigeria, the challenge is not only to develop mental health policies but also to ensure that research informs decisions, services reach people who need them and reforms translate into practical improvements in care. The Medical Director of the Federal Neuro-Psychiatric Hospital, Yaba, Dr Olugbenga Owoeye, said research was essential to improving clinical practice and strengthening the delivery of mental health services. He stressed the need to bridge the gap between research findings and their application, noting that studies should provide useful evidence for decision-making and improvements in patient care. The conference chairperson, Professor Mashudat Bello-Mojeed, also emphasised the need to strengthen mental health research and ensure that evidence played a greater role in shaping policies and reforms across Africa. She highlighted the importance of addressing the challenges confronting research development and building systems capable of supporting meaningful progress in mental healthcare. Another speaker, Dr Tolu Ajomale highlighted the role of legal and policy frameworks in addressing mental health challenges, pointing to the need for stronger links between legislation, institutional action and access to care. The discussions brought into focus the relationship between research, legislation and service delivery, with the experts calling for greater collaboration among governments, researchers and healthcare institutions. They said locally generated evidence could help identify the needs of African populations, guide the design of appropriate interventions and strengthen the continent’s response to mental health challenges. The conference called attention to the need for sustained investment in research and reforms that go beyond policy statements to deliver practical results. The experts insisted that mental health research must become a stronger foundation for policymaking, while existing laws and commitments must be translated into action that improves access to care. The post Psychiatrists seek home-grown research to tackle Africa’s mental health crisis appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: FG powers 2,214 homes, businesses with Kano mini-grids
items.description: By Obas Esiedesa, Abuja The Federal Government has commissioned two solar mini-grids in Kano State, providing 2,214 electricity connections to homes and businesses in underserved communities. The projects, delivered through the Rural Electrification Agency (REA) under the Distributed Access through Renewable Energy Scale-up (DARES) programme of the Nigeria Electrification Project (NEP), are funded by the World Bank. Located in Ballagaza, Gabasawa Local Government Area, and Marayar Rogo, Warawa Local Government Area, the facilities have a combined installed capacity of 268.4 kilowatt-peak (kWp). A statement by the REA on Thursday said the Ballagaza mini-grid has a capacity of 195.2kWp, while the Marayar Rogo facility has 73.2kWp. The projects have provided 1,564 electricity connections in Ballagaza and 650 in Marayar Rogo. Speaking at the commissioning, the Minister of Power, Chief Joseph Tegbe, said the projects demonstrated the importance of investment in renewable energy and collaboration with the private sector in expanding electricity access. He said the Federal Government would continue to encourage partnerships that accelerate the delivery of reliable and sustainable electricity, particularly to rural communities. According to him, the projects would bring electricity closer to underserved populations, support small businesses and create an enabling environment for economic growth. The REA said the mini-grids were expected to support productive activities, including milling, welding, tailoring, cold storage and other commercial services, improving business operations, productivity and household incomes. Representing Kano State Governor, the Managing Director of the Kano State Rural Electricity Board, Abba Kabir Yusuf, commended the Federal Government and the REA for extending electricity infrastructure to the benefiting communities. He said improved electricity supply would support commercial activities, enhance productivity and contribute to the state’s socio-economic development. The Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of the REA, Abba Abubakar Aliyu, said the agency’s objective went beyond installing electricity infrastructure to ensuring that communities derived tangible economic benefits from the projects. “With 2,214 connections across Ballagaza and Marayar Rogo, we are creating opportunities for households, supporting local businesses and providing a dependable foundation for productive work, stronger enterprises and improved incomes,” Aliyu said. He added that the agency remained committed to ensuring that electricity access translated into better livelihoods and economic opportunities for rural communities. The Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of Alfuttaim Nigeria Limited, Femi Kumuyi, whose company delivered the projects, said the facilities demonstrated the benefits of collaboration among the Federal Government, the REA, development partners and private-sector developers. He said the company would continue to support the expansion of reliable renewable energy solutions in underserved communities. The post FG powers 2,214 homes, businesses with Kano mini-grids appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Lula says rival should be disqualified over alleged Meta interference ahead of Brazil vote
items.description: Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s campaign has requested the disqualification of right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro in the lead up to the final round of the presidential election on Sunday over alleged interference by social media company Meta. In a petition filed to the country’s top electoral court on Wednesday, the leftist incumbent president accused Meta, the tech giant behind Whatsapp, Instagram and Facebook, of limiting its content to boost Bolsonaro’s campaign. In response, Bolsonaro filed a petition seeking to disqualify Lula over what he said was the mass dissemination of government posts on WhatsApp. The company has denied the campaigns have been treated unequally. It comes after UN experts said on Wednesday that they were concerned about reports of discrepancies in the ability of each campaign to reach voters on Meta’s platforms. A report led by the UN’s special rapporteur on freedom of expression said Meta must ensure a level playing field online during the election. It cited incidents including “temporary interruptions of one candidate’s campaign account; differences in audience engagement, user feeds, view counts and reach; restrictions on that campaign’s Instagram posts”. “Information, including from Meta employees, suggests that accounts linked to one side of the presidential race were disproportionately curtailed,” it read. Meta has denied taking action to favour one side of the election and has said it would comply with an order from a Brazilian court to treat Bolsonaro and Lula equally. Lula’s campaign had previously filed a complaint alleging that accounts and content related to Bolsonaro were boosted. Users also reported that Meta’s artificial intelligence tools were not generating images related to Lula. Pro-Lula supporters gathered outside Meta’s office in São Paulo on Monday, accusing the company of interference in the Brazilian electoral process Brazilians will head to the polls on Sunday as Lula seeks a fourth term in office. Bolsonaro beat Lula in the first round of voting on 4 October by a narrow margin, but fell short of the 50% of valid votes needed to win outright. On Wednesday, Lula’s campaign filed a petition to Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court (TSE) for Bolsonaro and Alfredo Gaspar, his candidate for vice-president, to be investigated over “abuse of economic power and improper use of social network”. The petition also seeks to make Bolsonaro ineligible to stand for election for eight years following the 2026 election. Meanwhile, Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of convicted former president Jair Bolsonaro, accused his rival of “abuse of political and economic power”. He claims the government has used personal data taken from official databases to send mass messages on Whatsapp to promote social programmes. Opinion polls suggest Sunday’s run-off will be extremely close, with little separating the two as Brazil’s 159 million registered voters prepare to go to the ballot boxes.

items.title: Hospitals deliberately targeted by Sudan’s RSF fighters, BBC investigation finds
items.description: A BBC investigation has found evidence that Sudanese paramilitary fighters systematically destroyed el-Fasher’s healthcare system during their long siege and subsequent takeover of the city in Darfur a year ago. UN human rights chief Volker Türk called the findings “deeply disturbing”, saying multiple attacks by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) on civilian infrastructure, including health facilities, were serious violations of international humanitarian law and may amount to war crimes. The RSF has rejected the BBC’s findings. The paramilitary group’s health minister described the allegations as propaganda and a deliberate attempt by the national army and its allies to smear the RSF’s reputation. Using sources who were on the ground in el-Fasher, the BBC has found details of at least 43 separate attacks on hospitals and healthcare sites from May 2024 to October 2025 – some hit multiple times. Under international law it is illegal to attack health facilities or their staff during conflict. The investigation also reveals the toll on medical workers in the western city. In the period from April 2023 to October 2025, the BBC’s data shows 120 were injured, 55 killed and 10 forcibly “disappeared” or abducted. “The RSF [were] trying to evacuate the hospitals, to put them out of service because the health system is the cornerstone of any city or any state,” says Dr Muhamed Suliman, a surgeon who was based in el-Fasher during the siege and spoke to the BBC. “The RSF started hitting these areas so citizens have no longer any way to stay there. It was intense. It was deliberate. It was planned.” The investigation comes a year after the fall of el-Fasher, one of the most brutal chapters of the civil war which erupted in April 2023 between the RSF and Sudan’s military. Both sides have been accused of attacks on health facilities. In March 2026, the World Health Organization (WHO) condemned the bombing of al-Daein hospital in RSF-held eastern Darfur, which killed dozens and forced the site to close. Sudan’s military is believed to have carried out the drone strikes, although it has denied responsibility. But events in el-Fasher represent “one of the clearest and most severe examples of the wider impact of the conflict on health care in Sudan,” the WHO said in response to a BBC query. UN investigators have reported that the fighting in el-Fasher bore the “hallmarks of genocide”, where historical ethnic animosities have seen Arab militias – now the backbone of RSF forces – target non-Arab groups such as those that populate the city. The BBC’s investigation reveals for the first time a detailed chronology of attacks on healthcare during the long siege of the city. Some medical facilities in el-Fasher closed down within weeks of the country’s civil war starting in April 2023. Crucially this included one of the main hospitals – the Teaching Hospital – located in a conflict zone in the middle of the city. Its operations were moved to el-Fasher’s South Hospital. There medical services continued, although increasingly hindered by power cuts and dwindling supplies. The situation changed dramatically a year later, when the RSF mounted its siege of el-Fasher. In late May and early June of 2024, the South Hospital was shelled several times as paramilitary fighters pushed forward from their positions in the east of the city. The first bombing came as a shock, says Dr Suliman. The area around the hospital that was hit was “very crowded because it was the only working hospital in the city providing surgical services”, he says. On that day medical staff operated on 16 injured patients, he added. The attacks culminated in an RSF raid on 8 June. Hospital staff were taken by surprise – many of them escaped over the back wall as the RSF fighters entered the building, says Dr Mustafa Ahmed, a pharmaceutical specialist. But the director general of the hospital, surgeon Izzeldin Ahmed Dawaud Asow, encountered a group of the paramilitaries outside his office. They did not know he was a doctor, he said, but denounced him with ethnic slurs. “There are no citizens here. You are Falangi,” they said, using a derogatory term implying that non-Arab Sudanese are foreigners. Dr Asow says he was beaten with rifle butts and lost consciousness at one point. Ultimately, he saved himself by pretending to be dead. “They put their hand on my chest, and I stopped breathing. And they said: ‘Leave him, leave him. The rubbish has died. Leave him.’ They left me.” That same day the RSF was driven out by the Sudanese military and its allies and Dr Asow returned to find the bodies of several patients and the surgical equipment in his operating room thoroughly destroyed, he said. The hospital closed and later fell into RSF hands when the army retreated. Dr Alaa Eldin Nugud, a prominent Sudanese surgeon who has joined the RSF-backed civilian government as health minister, insisted the South Hospital was being used as a military base. According to international law, hospitals can lose their protection if they are used by a party to the conflict to commit an “act harmful to the enemy”. In an interview with the BBC, Dr Nugud declared that missile launchers were set up on the grounds and shared a video showing remains of weapons filmed more than a year after the hospital closed, which he said supported his claim. He also showed us what he called maps of landmines planted around the Teaching Hospital, which is located next to Sudanese military headquarters. Doctors told us the hospital was not incorporated into the base and said they visited it to pick up medical equipment during the war. The BBC has found no independent evidence of Dr Nugud’s allegations. And the government of the Darfur region categorically rejected the charges. After the South Hospital shut, its staff and remaining equipment were moved to the Saudi Maternity Hospital in the west of the city, where the army had its main bases. Within days the pace of attacks on the facility picked up. At this stage the medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) sounded the alarm. “We do not know if hospitals are being intentionally targeted, but… the belligerents are not taking any precautions to spare them,” it said in a statement. However, in the course of our investigation we spoke to six doctors who described a pattern of systematic targeting. They told us how Saudi Hospital was repeatedly struck – on some days up to 25 times, with a mix of shelling and drones, the latter “intelligent rockets” with precision-guided attacks. Smaller medical facilities also came under fire. The BBC’s timeline records the steady closure of private hospitals and neighbourhood clinics. Furthermore, when some of these healthcare buildings shifted locations, the alternate venues were also attacked. The Specialised Children’s Hospital, which shut down at the beginning of the war along with the Teaching Hospital, moved to two other locations, both of which were then shelled and forced to close. Similarly, the main dialysis centre was struck and then attacked again after it relocated. By the time the RSF seized the city in October 2025, the Saudi Hospital was the only functioning health facility left. The medical staff there had rallied to try to keep working as conditions worsened. Doctors described how sandbags were set up to protect the building. They built underground bunkers out of steel containers and established a number of alternative sites to house and receive patients and conduct surgery as the threat of attacks and the damage to the main structure steadily increased. Dr Asow said this makeshift surgery was attacked five times in 2025. In one case, he says, he was operating on a patient’s neck when the building was shaken by an explosion – the medical staff ran out in fear, but he stayed. In another case, health workers had prepared the theatre for an operation, but he told them to move the patient elsewhere because it needed a deep clean given the relentless case load. Shortly afterward the room was destroyed by shells – and the patient survived. “From that day, some of my staff called me ‘Mr Deep Cleaning’ because they think that the issue of deep cleaning saved that patient,” he said. Dr Asow also describes how drones tracked the movement of patients. On 15 March 2025, people carrying the injured from the site of an attack to one of the temporary wards were followed by a hunting drone, he says. It struck as they reached the gate of the building, killing nine people. On 17 August of the same year a donkey cart was transferring patients to the alternative operating theatre because all the ambulances had been destroyed, Dr Asow told the BBC. It was hit by a drone, killing two patients, the driver and the donkey, he says. The RSF health minister dismissed these accounts as “a continuation of lies” by the military (SAF) and their local allies, known as the Joint Forces. “Even the medics, and many of the people who were there, because of this conflict, these tribal issues, these racial issues, they are allied with the Joint Forces and with the SAF. That’s why you don’t depend on that narrative,” he said. Doctors told the BBC they believed RSF fighters deliberately targeted medical facilities because army or allied fighters were among their patients. The onslaught of shelling and bombing culminated on 25 October 2025 with the RSF storming the hospital amid allegations of a massacre that killed more than 460 patients and their companions . The RSF has denied a massacre occurred, although the WHO condemned the reported killings and satellite imagery appeared to show clusters of bodies on the blood-soaked grounds of the hospital. The BBC shared details of its investigation with the UN human rights chief, who said our findings were “deeply disturbing”, and consistent with the analysis of his office. “Our monitoring and documentation shows the RSF repeatedly struck el-Fasher’s main hospitals and makeshift health facilities, destroying or seriously damaging them and severely impacting access to health services for thousands of civilians trapped in the city,” Türk said. Healthcare in el-Fasher is now being run by the RSF-backed government. It has released several videos showing the Saudi Hospital and the Teaching Hospital re-opened, cleaned up and seeing some patients. Dr Nugud says South Hospital is also set to reopen. He denied that doctors were forcibly abducted, telling the BBC that instead they had chosen to stay on to work. “I have a video in front of the children’s hospital when we freed a consultant, a doctor and six of the medical staff who were working with the SAF, and then when el-Fasher got liberated, there was a forgiveness for all of them. “We liberated them,” he said. The BBC spoke to one of the doctors in the video, Dr Al-Haj Mohamed Ahmed. He told us he had no choice: “I was forced to be there. “If I spoke out of line, they’d put a bullet through my head.” He was among several medical workers captured while trying to escape the city and sent back, along with Dr Mustafa Ahmed. They distinguished themselves by bringing a cholera epidemic in a temporary prison at the paediatric hospital under control and were subsequently taken to Saudi Hospital. “They started to say that you are the people of the city, and we take the city, so we need to work together for the sake of the city,” says Dr Mustafa Ahmed, who describes waking up several mornings in a row at the prison to find 50 inmates dead of cholera. A year on from the fall of el-Fasher, the trauma of this dark period in Sudan’s civil war is still painfully sharp. The front lines have shifted elsewhere with no signs of a resolution to the conflict. And attacks on healthcare continue as part of a wider and devastating humanitarian crisis.

items.title: Free digital learning reaches 1m Nigerian students — UNICEF, Airtel
items.description: … As partnership connects nearly 2,000 schools, trains over 19,000 teachers By Chioma Obinna Nearly one million Nigerian students across the country are benefiting from free digital learning opportunities through a partnership between Airtel Africa, the United Nations Children’s Fund, UNICEF, and the Federal Government, as stakeholders move to bridge the digital divide and equip young people with skills for future employment. The initiative, which has connected nearly 2,000 schools and reached more than 20,000 teachers, is removing data-cost barriers to digital education through free access to learning platforms, while equipping students with digital literacy, artificial intelligence, entrepreneurship, and employability skills. The impact of the programme came into focus during a joint Airtel Africa-UNICEF delegation’s assessment tour of selected schools and youth programmes in Lagos, where students demonstrated how technology is changing their learning experience and opening new opportunities beyond the classroom. The delegation, led by Garreth Spillane, Chief of Staff to the Chairman of Airtel Africa, visited Government Senior College, Agege; St George’s U.N.A. Primary School, Ipaja; and Yaba College of Technology, where students, teachers and young people showcased the practical benefits of digital learning and skills acquisition. At Government Senior College, students demonstrated how digital learning tools, including artificial intelligence, are supporting classroom activities, while young people at Yaba College of Technology showed how digital platforms are helping them develop skills for employment, entrepreneurship and self-reliance. Speaking during the tour, UNICEF Deputy Representative in Nigeria, Dr Rownak Khan, said free access to digital learning was helping young people acquire the knowledge and skills needed to prepare for their future. “I’m very impressed to see how these girls are learning digital skills, and I really would like to thank the Ministry of Education at both the federal and state levels,” Khan said. “But our biggest appreciation goes to Airtel Nigeria for this partnership. Airtel has supported us with zero-rating, providing free access so these girls can learn the skills they need to prepare for school and their future careers.” She said the initiative was particularly important for girls, children with disabilities and learners in underserved communities, who must not be left behind as education increasingly embraces technology. “Access to free digital learning not only bridges the digital divide but also brings children and young people closer to the knowledge, skills and opportunities they need to shape their and their country’s future,” Khan said. “Our partnership with Airtel and the Government of Nigeria is supporting teachers and creating pathways from learning to earning. Girls, children with disabilities and those in underserved communities must be among the first to benefit.” The Nigeria Learning Passport, one of the programme’s major platforms, provides online, mobile and offline access to curriculum-aligned educational resources for pre-primary, primary and secondary school pupils. The platform hosts more than 15,000 educational resources, including lessons in English, Hausa, Igbo and Yoruba. It has recorded more than 2.5 million registered students and nearly 100,000 registered teachers. The initiative, introduced in Nigeria during the COVID-19 pandemic when school closures disrupted learning nationwide, is now hosted by the Federal Ministry of Education as part of efforts to expand access to educational resources. Through the partnership, Airtel provides zero-rated access to the Nigeria Learning Passport, the ministry’s Inspire and Ignite platforms, the Digital National Education Management Information System and the Youth Agency Marketplace, also known as YOMA. The arrangement allows users to access the designated platforms without incurring mobile data charges, addressing one of the major obstacles to digital learning for families with limited resources. Head of Programmes at the Airtel Africa Foundation, Esi Asare Prah, said digital inclusion in education was central to preparing young Africans for an increasingly technology-driven world. “One of the biggest missions for the foundation is driving faster digital inclusion in education to improve learning outcomes,” Prah said. “For Airtel as an organisation, digital inclusion is a major priority. We want to ensure that young people across Africa are equipped for the future.” She said the visit demonstrated how access to digital resources could help young learners, particularly girls, gain confidence in technology and develop practical skills. “It was wonderful to see young girls taking full advantage of the opportunity afforded by the zero-rated Learning Passport,” she said. “Because they can learn free of charge, they are able to absorb information and, within minutes, develop content from what they’ve learned.” Prah said the Airtel Africa Foundation was committed to strengthening digital infrastructure, expanding access in underserved rural communities, empowering marginalised groups and promoting long-term educational equity. She added that young people across Nigeria with an Airtel connection could access the Nigeria Learning Passport free of charge. For students, the benefits extend beyond lessons delivered in school. The Head Girl of Government Senior College, Tosin Adeola, said the platform had improved students’ academic performance and study habits by allowing them to revisit lessons and review difficult topics at home. She thanked UNICEF and Airtel for providing the opportunity, saying students were determined to make effective use of the platform. Airtel Africa Foundation committee member, Spillane, said connectivity could transform education when it enabled students to access quality learning materials and teachers to use digital tools effectively. “Connectivity brings transformative opportunities when it helps students access quality digital learning and enables teachers to use digital tools effectively, as we’ve seen demonstrated so ably here in Nigeria,” he said. “Working with UNICEF and governments, we will continue to connect schools, remove data-cost barriers through zero-rated learning platforms and support teachers across the continent.” The Minister of State for Education, Prof. Suwaiba Sa’idu Ahmad, said collaboration among government, development partners and telecommunications providers was necessary to improve learning outcomes and ensure that digital education reached children regardless of their location. “Transforming education in Nigeria requires strong partnerships aligned with government priorities and learners’ needs,” Ahmad said. “We must strengthen teachers’ capacity, expand access to quality digital content, protect children online and ensure digital learning reaches every child, wherever they live.” In Abuja, the delegation also met with the Office of the Vice President and the Federal Ministry of Education to discuss reliable connectivity, quality learning content, teacher training, inclusive digital design, stronger education data systems, child online safety and sustainable financing. The partners reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening these areas to improve learning outcomes and expand access to digital education. Across 13 African countries, the five-year Airtel Africa-UNICEF partnership has connected more than 3,000 schools, provided zero-rated access to more than 60 learning platforms and reached over 2.5 million children. The partners said continued collaboration with governments would be critical to expanding the initiative and ensuring that more children and young people, particularly those in underserved communities, could benefit from digital learning and the opportunities it creates. items.title: Forces armées nationales : 24 officiers en administration reçoivent leur diplôme
items.description: Les Forces armées nationales ont organisé une cérémonie de fin de formation des officiers stagiaires du premier cours de perfectionnement en administration et du deuxième cours d’application des officiers en administration, le jeudi 22 octobre 2026, à Ouagadougou. Onze officiers stagiaires du premier cours de perfectionnement en administration et treize officiers stagiaires dont quatre femmes, du deuxième cours d’application des officiers en administration des Forces armées nationales ont fini leur formation. La cérémonie de sortie des promotions a eu lieu, le jeudi 22 octobre 2026, sous la présidence du directeur central de l’intendance militaire, l’intendant lieutenant-colonel Issa Konseiga. Pour le porte-parole des stagiaires, le commandant Yannick Cheick Kader Sourweima, le stage de perfectionnement en intendance a permis à des officiers chevronnés de réinterroger leurs pratiques, d’intégrer les nouvelles exigences de la gestion publique et d’adapter leurs compétences aux défis opérationnels contemporains. Quant au cours d’application des officiers d’administration, d’après lui, la promotion a suivi un cursus exhaustif de cours magistraux, de travaux dirigés, de conférences et d’immersion. Il a poursuivi que l’objectif assigné était de former des gestionnaires immédiatement opérationnels, capables d’administrer un corps de troupes, d’assurer la comptabilité des deniers et des matières et de soutenir le combattant avec rigueur et efficacité. Ils sont 24 cadres compétents à renforcer les effectifs dans l’administration de l’armée. Le président de la cérémonie, le directeur central de l’intendance militaire, l’intendant lieutenant-colonel Issa Konseiga, a, pour sa part, exprimé sa satisfaction pour cette fin de stage. Pour lui, la proclamation des résultats et la remise des diplômes consacrent les efforts des stagiaires et traduisent la volonté de renforcer les compétences nécessaires à l’efficacité du soutien aux Forces armées nationales. Ainsi, il a adressé ses chaleureuses félicitations aux récipiendaires. Toutefois, il a laissé entendre que le diplôme atteste les connaissances acquises, mais que c’est la qualité du service rendu qui révèle la véritable valeur professionnelle. En outre, le directeur Issa Konseiga a fait savoir que l’intendance militaire occupe une place essentielle dans la préparation et la conduite des opérations, car derrière chaque unité engagée, se trouvent des ressources à mobiliser, des besoins à anticiper, des approvisionnements à assurer et des droits à préserver. « La performance opérationnelle ne dépend donc pas uniquement de la qualité des équipements et de la détermination des combattants, elle repose également sur la fiabilité du soutien, la disponibilité des ressources et la rigueur de leur gestion », a-t-il expliqué. Car, a-t-il estimé, le soutien ne s’improvise pas, il se planifie, s’organise et se perfectionne grâce à des personnels compétents et responsables. Evariste YODA

items.title: GES directs schools to enforce the Code of Conduct’s ban on students doing chores at teachers’ bungalows
items.description: The Ghana Education Service (GES) has directed all senior high schools to immediately comply with an existing provision in its Code of Conduct that prohibits students from performing household chores at the bungalows of teachers and headteachers. The Service says the practice, which is already prohibited under the Code of Conduct, must stop with immediate effect. GES Director-General, Professor Ernest Kofi Davis, gave the directive in an interview with JoyNews’ Naa Dedei Tettey on Thursday, October 22, 2026. Professor Davis explained that the Code of Conduct, under Section 3.7 V, explicitly states that students are not expected to be asked to engage in household chores. “We are going to write to schools to make sure that it doesn’t happen because in our code of conduct, section 3.7 V, it is written that the students are not expected to be asked to engage in household chores,” he said. “We are going to write today. By the end of the week, we expect it to get to our schools.” He said he expected the directive to reach all regional directors by Friday, October 23, 2026. “I expect the news to get to all regional directors to remind our staff to apprise themselves with the code of conduct and cease inviting students to schools to do household chores because the code of conduct does not permit that,” he stated. When asked why the practice had been happening despite the Code of Conduct, Professor Davis said: “So, that’s why we are saying they should apprise themselves of that. It’s not acceptable. So, we’ll remind them.” The directive follows growing concerns about the welfare of students in senior high schools, particularly in the wake of the Obuasi SHTS sexual abuse allegations. The practice of students performing household chores at teachers’ bungalows has long been a subject of debate in Ghana, with critics arguing that it exposes students to exploitation and abuse. The GES Code of Conduct explicitly prohibits the practice, but enforcement has been inconsistent. The GES is expected to communicate the directive to all regional directors by Friday, October 23, 2026. Regional directors will then be responsible for ensuring that schools under their jurisdiction comply with the existing Code of Conduct. The Service has emphasised that the practice is not acceptable and that staff must familiarize themselves with the Code of Conduct.

items.title: ‎First Lady receives China’s Ambassador in Aso Villa
items.description: ‎–Says friendship between two nations has begun to yield visible results ‎ ‎By Johnbosco Agbakwuru ‎ ‎ABUJA — THE First Lady, Senator Oluremi Tinubu on Thursday, received the Chinese Ambassador to Nigeria, ‎Yu Dunhai at the presidential villa, Abuja. ‎ ‎At the visit, Ambassador Dunhai said the ongoing reforms in Nigeria, under President Bola Tinubu’s Renewed Hope Agenda are yielding tangible and life-changing results that should be consolidated beyond 2027. ‎ ‎The Ambassador said having seen the half year trade volume between the two countries grow to 18 billion dollars and having watched Nigeria in the last three years take a new shape, on strong macroeconomic footing, the country must continue the path by putting their faith in ongoing reforms. ‎ ‎Yu Dunhai noted that the there is renewed and stronger confidence by foreign investors and his country will not shy away from the keying into this. ‎ ‎The envoy pointed out that in the last three years, Nigeria’s export to China has increased tremendously. ‎ ‎He said in deepening the bilateral relations between the two countries, China will ensure to work with the principle that Africa’s resources belong to Africa, stick to high quality investment, make use of domestic human capital among others. ‎ ‎He explained that the visit, being his first since assuming office in Nigeria two years ago, is to convey his government’s admiration for the Renewed Hope Agenda, ably complemented by the First Lady’s Renewed Hope Initiative, and to explore further areas of support, particularly in health, education and promoting food security. ‎ ‎Responding the First Lady of Nigeria Senator Tinubu noted that an endorsement for a second term in office for President Tinubu, from a strong ally such as China is cheering. ‎ ‎She commended China’s interest in the agricultural sector, especially with a promise to collaborate on use of technology to enhance food security. ‎ ‎The First Lady promised to encourage a collaboration with the Federal Ministry of Agriculture and Food Security. ‎ ‎“When friendship have transcended this long, it begins to yield results and we are beginning to see the results now”. ‎ ‎“We are looking for how the vulnerable ones would be lifted, we know this will help us a lot. Nigeria is transforming. And we must embrace the new Nigeria”. ‎ ‎Nigeria and China elevated their bilateral relations to a comprehensive strategic partnership, since year 2024 during President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s state visit to China. items.title: Crowd of 50 beats foreigner to death in South Africa
items.description: A foreign national has been beaten to death by a crowd of about 50 people in Durban, South Africa, police say. According to police, the unidentified man, believed to be in his late 30s or early 40s, was first approached by two men by the roadside before being assaulted by a larger group. He was pronounced dead at the scene. Police have launched an investigation into the murder, with the motive yet to be established. The killing follows a wave of protests against immigrants in South Africa this year, some of which have turned violent. Earlier this month, shops and cars were set on fire in Durban, as well as Soweto, near Johannesburg. Provincial police spokesperson Robert Netshiunda told the BBC they cannot speculate on the motive for the killing in Durban and that more information would be shared once verified. The government has urged demonstrators to act peacefully while also acknowledging the need for immigration reforms. It says tens of thousands of foreign nationals have been deported or repatriated since it launched a crackdown earlier this year. One of the groups behind the protests, March and March, initially set a 30 June deadline for all undocumented migrants to leave South Africa. Several protests were held ahead of that deadline, with reports of attacks on people from other African countries. These prompted several countries, including Zimbabwe, Nigeria and Ghana, to take steps to repatriate their citizens amid fears of further violence. Nigeria accused South African authorities of responsibility for the deaths of two of its citizens that month. Ghana also confirmed the death of a citizen, Bashiru Isak, a father of three who was fatally shot in Cape Town during demonstrations targeting foreign nationals. His death led to a diplomatic row with South Africa, which said the scale of the violence had been exaggerated. One of the leaders of the March and March movement, Jacinta Ngobese-Zuma, denied that she was xenophobic. “We can’t be living with these people for so many years and now when we say it is too much, it is enough, we are told that we are xenophobic,” she told the BBC’s Focus on Africa programme. South Africa has struggled with xenophobic attacks for nearly two decades. In 2008, more than 60 people were killed and tens of thousands displaced during widespread attacks on foreign nationals. The latest unrest comes against a backdrop of widespread poverty, deep inequality and unemployment affecting roughly a third of the workforce. Migrants are frequently accused of taking jobs, contributing to crime and placing pressure on public services, although researchers say such sweeping claims are not supported by evidence. Despite its economic difficulties, South Africa remains one of the continent’s main destinations for migrants seeking employment, safety and better opportunities.
